lesson: 2

::: {.lead}
Today you test an AI assistant like a scientist: you give it jobs, you
record its answers, and you check them with other tools. Do each experiment
when your teacher shows it. After each step, write your result in its box.
At the end, copy your key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a lab computer with a browser, an AI assistant that the
  university allows (for example `copilot.microsoft.com` with your
  university account), a search engine (`bing.com`) and a calculator.
- **Time:** about 40 minutes for the three experiments.
- **Never type personal data** (your ID number, phone or address) into the
  AI assistant.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. On the
  interactive lesson, every step has "Check your result". Look only after
  you try.

## Experiment 1 · Two good jobs

**Aim:** see two jobs that AI does well, and check the result.
*(Lesson notes 2.1 · about 12 minutes)*

1. Ask the AI assistant: *Give me 5 ideas for a one-day class trip in
   Jordan.*

   {{< record "Two of the ideas" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good result: five different places for one day, for example Jerash,
   Ajloun, the Dead Sea, Petra and Wadi Rum. Ideas are a good job for AI:
   you choose the best ones.
   :::

2. Ask: *Sum up this text in 3 points:* and paste the text below.

   > The college library has new rules from Sunday 1 November. It opens at
   > 8 a.m. and closes at 4 p.m., Sunday to Thursday. Students can borrow
   > three books for two weeks. Phones must be silent in the reading room.
   > The library also has ten new computers. To use one, students show
   > their university card at the desk.

   {{< record "The three points" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good summary: the library opens 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Sunday to Thursday;
   students borrow three books for two weeks; ten new computers, with the
   university card. (Silent phones may replace one point.)
   :::

3. Read the summary again, point by point. Did the AI add a fact that is
   **not** in the text?

   {{< record "A fact that is not in the text (or: none)" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Often **none**, but sometimes the AI adds something, for example "the
   library is free" or "it opens on Saturday". Delete every fact that is not
   in the text: you are responsible for what you use.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · Test the weak spots

**Aim:** catch a wrong number and an invented book, the way a checker does.
*(Lesson notes 2.2 · about 14 minutes)*

1. Ask: *How much are 12 pens at 0.25 JD each?* Then work it out with the
   calculator.

   {{< record "AI answer … ; calculator …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The calculator gives **3.00 JD** (12 × 0.25). Many AI answers are right
   here, but some give another number. For exact numbers, use a calculator
   or a spreadsheet: a wrong number is a weak spot of AI.
   :::

2. Ask: *Give me 3 books about Microsoft Excel, with the author and the
   year.* Search for each title in `bing.com`.

   {{< record "Book 1 … , book 2 … , book 3 … (found / not found)" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A typical result: one or two books are found, but often one book is not
   found, or it has another author or year. A book that no search finds is
   a **hallucination**: the AI invented it.
   :::

3. Play **Weak Spots** on the interactive lesson: read each AI answer and
   choose its weak spot.

   {{< record "My score … of 7" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The seven answers: two invented facts (a book, an award), old
   information (an app version), a wrong number (12 pens), bias (the nurse
   is "she"), missing context (the homework topic) and one good draft.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · The right tool

**Aim:** choose AI, a search engine or a spreadsheet for a job, and compare
an AI answer with the real source. *(Lesson notes 2.3 · about 12 minutes)*

1. Ask the AI assistant: *What are the opening hours of the library of
   Al-Israa University?*

   {{< record "The AI says" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Any answer here needs a check: the AI may give hours from an old page, or
   invent them, and it sounds sure either way.
   :::

2. Open the university website and look for the library or its opening
   hours. Which answer do you trust?

   {{< record "I trust … , because …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good answer: "I trust the university website. It is the official
   source, and it is up to date." If the website does not show the hours,
   the next source is the library itself (a phone call or the notice at the
   door), not the AI.
   :::

3. Play **Right Tool** on the interactive lesson. Then write the tool for
   each job: the last day to pay the fees, the total of 40 prices, a polite
   reminder e-mail.

   {{< record "Fees … ; 40 prices … ; e-mail …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **A search engine** and the official university website (dates and
   rules), **a spreadsheet** (it adds exactly), **an AI assistant** (a
   draft that you read and change).
   :::
